entries.title: 2 hospitalized after small plane crash in Bolingbrook
entries.summary: <p>Two people were hospitalized after a small plane crashed in a Bolingbrook park Tuesday night, according to the Bolingbrook Fire Department.</p><p>Around 6:29 p.m., the plane crashed in Indian Chase Meadows Park shortly after taking off from Bolingbrook Clow International Airport and attempting to return to the airport, according to Bolingbrook fire officials and Federal Aviation Administration flight data. </p><p>The only two occupants of the aircraft were taken to Good Samaritan Hospital in stable condition. No other injuries were reported. </p><p>The FAA and the National Transportation Safety Board are investigating the incident, according to Bolingbrook officials.</p><p>The plane, a 1978-built Cessna 152, is registered to JW Aviation Chicago Flight Training School, according to FAA records. The Bolingbrook-based flight school didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.</p>

entries.title: Rookie lefty Hagen Smith sets up White Sox with three scoreless innings in Game 1 win
entries.summary: <p>HOUSTON — Hagen Smith had no idea how long he’d pitch to open Game 1 of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox’</a> wild-card series Tuesday against the Astros.</p><p>“Just go out there until they told me not to,” he said.</p><p>Manager Will Venable revealed that the plan was for the rookie left-hander to face 11 batters. That’s exactly what he did in three scoreless innings, setting up the Sox for a 6-3 victory that put them one win from advancing to the American League Division Series.</p><p>“It couldn’t have gone better as far as him setting the tone for the guys, coming in and attacking zone, getting swing and miss,” Venable said. “Did a great job to put us in a really good spot to continue in the middle part of that game.”</p><p>Smith began a bullpen game by allowing only two hits, walking none and striking out two. He threw 38 pitches, 28 for strikes.</p><p>“Kyle [Teel] did a great job calling the game for me,” Smith said. “Just attacking with everything. A lot of cutters and sliders, just stacking those a lot early and heaters here and there.”</p><p>“The newness is always tough,” said Astros manager Joe Espada, whose team faced Smith for the first time. “Kind of crossfire, tough angle. His pitches do have some difficult shapes that keep you off-balance. He did a nice of doing that.”</p><p>It continued a run of strong showings by Smith, who had a 1.29 ERA in 18 regular-season outings, one of them to start a game and another to finish a game. In 28 innings, he allowed 11 hits, walked 16 and struck out 41.</p><p>The Sox chose him to open because of the Astros’ No. 2 hitter, the left-handed Yordan Alvarez. He’s the leading candidate to win the AL MVP Award after hitting 42 home runs and leading the majors in batting average (.316), on-base percentage (.432) and slugging percentage (.601).</p><p>Smith retired him twice, on grounders to second and third.</p><p>“You circle him as one of the guys that you try not to let him beat you,” Smith said. “Just try to do the same thing I always do: not make the moment too big for that certain hitter and attack him with my strengths.”</p><p>After Smith, the Sox used Jordan Hicks, Sean Newcomb, David Sandlin and Grant Taylor. Though Newcomb allowed a two-run homer to Nelson Velazquez in the fifth, they all flummoxed the Astros.</p><p>“I thought that was the difference in the game,” Espada said. “They gave us different arms, different arm angles. They displayed different repertoires. I thought they did a nice job of mixing and matching, and we just couldn’t get anything going.”</p><p>Sean Burke will try to keep the Astros in check when he starts Game 2 on Wednesday. With the bullpen accounting for all nine innings Tuesday, the Sox could use a long outing from Burke, who has pitched at least seven innings five times this season.</p>

entries.title: After a prospect path marked by injury, White Sox starter Sean Burke is grateful for postseason opportunity
entries.summary: <p>HOUSTON — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox’</a> pursuit of a division title means <b>Sean Burke</b> pitched on Friday, and wasn’t available to start Game 1 of the wild card series.</p><p>The White Sox’ MLB-leading use of openers means that Burke had a long wait to be named the starter of Game 2. But after running a 3.34 ERA in a career-high 172⅓ innings this year, as far as the Sox rotation goes this postseason: he’s their guy.</p><p>And it matters to him, perhaps as much as anything.</p><p>“This is my life,” Burke told the Sun-Times. “I don't have family, no girl, no kids. This is all I do.”</p><p>Rather than pressure, the feeling Burke expressed while leaning against the railing of the visitors dugout in Daikin Park was gratitude. He posted a 7.61 ERA in limited innings at Triple-A in 2023 while his shoulder barked, and his velocity lagged.</p><p>While 2024 would ultimately be the year he made a major-league debut that launched him into the White Sox rotation, it also saw a recurrence of shoulder discomfort at one point.</p><p>“I knew I was good, it was more am I ever gonna get my arm feeling good enough to be myself and pitch how I know I can pitch again,” Burke said.</p><p>Comparatively, righting his control after two late-season stinkers, ahead of a chance to close out the White Sox’ first playoff series victory in 21 years is less of a concern. After temporarily scrapping it to save bullets, Burke re-introduced his long-toss routine, which alleviated his fastball cutting unexpectedly. He re-emphasized his cutter as another strike-grabbing pitch outside his fastball.</p><p>It hasn’t made him infallible on the mound. He wants to kick his tick of reacting to every hard-hit ball driven in the air like it’s about to travel 500 feet. But it has him and the Sox confident he’s back to someone the team can trust in its biggest spot in years. That’s something to be grateful for, especially from his perspective.</p><p>“[In 2023], this team was bad, I wasn't even pitching,” Burke said. “So there was no real vision of this. To have this be the result of that work for me is cool.”</p><h3><b>Smith sharp in start</b></h3><h3></h3><p>In his 28-inning debut season out of the bullpen, <b>Hagen Smith </b>ran a 1.29 ERA, so all his outings were <i>good</i>. But the second inning of work is where his arm slot would dip, and walks became an issue.</p><p>“The arm was getting a little lower, kind of getting scoopier, not able to drive stuff to the right locations,” said pitching coach <b>Zach Bove</b>. “Part of it is just getting used to the [relief] role. Managing the adrenaline, and where you get up and then sit down and get back up.”</p><p>He looked used to it opening up the Sox’ bullpen game-led 6-3 victory on Tuesday, stringing together three walk-free, scoreless innings. Most vitally, he induced two weak groundouts from fearsome Astros slugger <b>Yordan Alvarez</b>.</p><h3><b>Intentional obstruction</b></h3><p><b>Sam Antonacci </b>running in the path of <b>Christian Walker</b>’s throw to second base in the first inning, triggering a deflection that granted him an extra base, so he could later score on a sacrifice fly?</p><p>The Sox teach that.</p><p>“That's a baserunning fundamental that these guys are aware of and implement when the time is appropriate,” said <b>Will Venable</b> when <b>Tristan Peters</b> did it earlier this month in Cleveland.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/29/chicago-white-sox-mlb-playoffs-postseason-houston-astros-wild-card-chris-getz-miguel-vargas-chase-meidroth-kyle-teel-colson-montgomery" >Whatever happens, White Sox in better shape than after their last playoff series vs. Astros</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/29/white-sox-hold-on-for-6-3-victory-over-astros-in-game-1-of-wild-card-series-will-venable-grant-taylor-sam-antonacci-kyle-teel-colson-montgomery" >White Sox hold on for 6-3 victory over Astros in Game 1 of wild card series</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Grant Taylor's 'heroic' relief effort puts White Sox on brink of ALDS
entries.summary: <p>HOUSTON — As Grant Taylor reached back for each of the 54 pitches he used to nail down the final seven outs of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox’</a> first road playoff victory in six years, he called upon a higher power to get him through it, to add an extra tick to his triple-digit velocity, to get his — at times — wayward fastball in the zone.</p><p>“Just kind of praying to God,” Taylor said. “I'm gonna give you everything I got, if you give me everything you got.”</p><p>To lock down a 6-3 win in Houston that put them a win away from the franchise’s first postseason series victory since winning the World Series in 2005 in this same ballpark, the best option the White Sox could call upon was Taylor. Even up four runs in the seventh after putting consistent pressure on a leaky Astros bullpen game early, manager Will Venable called for Taylor with two outs and a runner on second in the seventh.</p><p>When it comes to securing a victory in a best-of-three series, there’s no room for half-measures.</p><p>“Heroic,” Venable said of Taylor’s effort. “There was a case to be made [for Taylor to] start that seventh inning. But just where we were at with a little bit of space, wanted to see if we could kick the can down the road and just get as many out as we could with [David] Sandlin. And then once they had a runner at second base, we wanted to just shut it down.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Grant Taylor’s 54 pitches were his most since April of 2025 in AA. That outing was a start, obviously <a href="https://t.co/4N6VhdpdPE">pic.twitter.com/4N6VhdpdPE</a></p>— James Fegan (@JRFegan) <a href="https://x.com/JRFegan/status/2105102851370614818?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 30, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Taylor’s fastball command made it “more of a chase” pitch in catcher Kyle Teel’s description, as he waded through the vaunted top of the Astros order in the eighth. He yielded a run when Jeremy Pena and Yordan Alvarez strung together one-out singles, and after striking out Isaac Paredes, Astros legend Jose Altuve poked a full-count slider down the third base line and reached first just as Miguel Vargas’ errant throw dragged Munetaka Murakami off the bag.</p><p>The play drew Astros catcher Yainer Diaz to the plate as the tying run, and brought an oft-moody Daikin Park crowd to a full boil for the first and last time on the evening. It was there where the quirk of the burly right-hander with triple-digit heat having better feel for his breaking stuff on this day played in the Sox’ favor. Taylor’s full-count curveball on the outside corner froze Diaz for strike three, and froze any Astros’ comeback hopes in place–after Taylor came out and pitched the ninth as well.</p><p>“It's a trait of a really, really good pitcher,” Teel said of Taylor fending off Astros hitters without his best fastball command.</p><p>“I’m being honest, I don’t know what I threw,” Taylor said of the curve to Diaz, while still vibrating with adrenaline in the postgame locker room. “A couple guys coming up that are pretty good hitters, tying run on deck, that's probably going to take the cake for best curveball [of my career], just because of the situation.”</p><p>The situation wound up calling on Taylor to use the most pitches he’s thrown in a game since April of 2025, when he was working as a starter for the Double-A Birmingham Barons. He dealt with soreness while recovering from starts back then, and the same nutty athleticism that allows him to release the ball more than seven feet out from the pitching rubber made Sox officials wonder how much Taylor could hold up long-term. They chose to move him to the major-league bullpen with a quickness and let him fire his best bullets when it mattered most.</p><p>With five strikeouts to put the Sox within a game of a Division Series rematch with the rival Guardians, the obvious question comes after Taylor extended himself like never before: can he do it again? And how soon?</p><p>“Ideally, tomorrow,” Taylor said. “I'm going to give this team everything I've got. They've given me everything they've got, so I'm gonna do everything I can to be there.”</p><p></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/29/chicago-white-sox-mlb-playoffs-postseason-houston-astros-wild-card-chris-getz-miguel-vargas-chase-meidroth-kyle-teel-colson-montgomery" >Whatever happens, White Sox in better shape than after their last playoff series vs. Astros</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/29/white-sox-hold-on-for-6-3-victory-over-astros-in-game-1-of-wild-card-series-will-venable-grant-taylor-sam-antonacci-kyle-teel-colson-montgomery" >White Sox hold on for 6-3 victory over Astros in Game 1 of wild card series</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Whatever happens, White Sox in better shape than after their last playoff series vs. Astros
entries.summary: <p>HOUSTON — There's something very familiar about all this.</p><p>Almost five years ago, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> were in this ballpark, playing the Astros in the American League Division Series. The Sox had won the Central, continuing the success they built in the pandemic-shortened 2020 season, when they made the wild-card round.</p><p>But the Sox lost the first two games in Houston, won a memorable Game 3 at home, then were blown out two nights later. Though they were outclassed, the Sox saw better days ahead, with a core of Tim Anderson, Yoan Moncada and Luis Robert Jr. expected to take another step.</p><p>The only step they took was backward. All three of them plummeted in performance, manager Tony La Russa’s return blew up in chairman Jerry Reinsdorf’s face and the team dropped from 93 victories to 81.</p><p>It wasn’t a collapse, but it felt like a gut punch to fans, who broke 2 million in attendance for the first time since 2011. What followed were the first consecutive seasons with at least 100 losses in the team’s 126-year history — three, to be exact, including an MLB-record 121 losses in ’24.</p><p>Fast-forward to today. The Sox followed an encouraging finish to 2025 — their second-half run differential was plus-3, a bit better than their first-half number of minus-98 — with an unlikely run to the playoffs in which they occupied first place for 96 days.</p><p>Yes, it should’ve been more, and they should’ve won the division, in which case they would’ve been relaxing at home and resting a worn-out pitching staff for the next round. But after all that losing, it’s hard to quibble with a playoff berth of any kind.</p><p>And this, too, should be the beginning of better days for the Sox, with a core of Miguel Vargas, Chase Meidroth and Kyle Teel expected to take another step. However this wild-card series goes — and it got off to a great start with a 6-3 victory in Game 1 on Tuesday — the Sox are in better shape than they were in 2022.</p><p>“We feel like we’re still just getting started,” general manager Chris Getz said.</p><p>And with good reason. An overcrowded Dodgers system made Vargas available for the taking, and he has turned into the power hitter he was believed to be. The Sox think Meidroth could win a batting title, and they love Teel so much that it seems they’d wait out countless injuries to get him in the lineup.</p><p>After piecing together a rotation for much of the season, the Sox have arms on the way. Hagen Smith already is here but not in the role he eventually will hold. He’s excelling as a long reliever — or opener, as was the case Tuesday, when he threw three scoreless innings — but will be stretched out to start next season. Noah Schultz is expected to join him in the rotation.</p><p>The Sox aren’t short on position-player prospects, either. Shortstop Roch Cholowsky, the No. 1 pick in the draft, could be with the team next season. Infielder Caleb Bonemer, who totaled 37 home runs at two minor-league levels this season, could be up the year after. Shortstop Billy Carlson could follow. All are ranked in the top 60 of all prospects, according to MLB.com.</p><p>“You look at the amount of years that we’re going to have ahead of us with a lot of the player group that we have,” Getz said. “And we’ll look to add, and we’ll look to get these guys better.”</p><p>One of those players who needs to get better is Colson Montgomery, who set the major-league record for strikeouts in a season this year with 227 — more than 35% of his plate appearances. He has stayed in the lineup — he batted ninth for the first time all season Tuesday — in case he gets a hold of one, which he actually did in the fourth inning. It was his first homer since Sept. 5.</p><p>Montgomery hasn’t even played two full seasons yet, but he’ll have plenty of competition from those prospects. The Sox’ first-round pick in 2021, Montgomery ranked second among all shortstops with 31 homers, and the team likes his defense. But unless he’s going to hit 61 homers, he can’t be Adam Dunn at shortstop.</p><p>But there are worse problems for the Sox to have — and they’ve had them. Getz is looking pretty good for not going all in at the trade deadline. It ended up being a win-win — make the playoffs and keep your top prospects.</p><p>“I think that’s well said,” Getz said. “We certainly didn’t want to mortgage the future. And we were able to get players with control that have helped our major-league club do what they’ve done. Just continue to find ways to get this group better.”</p><p>It’s already pretty good.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/29/white-sox-hold-on-for-6-3-victory-over-astros-in-game-1-of-wild-card-series-will-venable-grant-taylor-sam-antonacci-kyle-teel-colson-montgomery" >White Sox hold on for 6-3 victory over Astros in Game 1 of wild card series</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/29/white-sox-fans-are-all-in-on-long-postseason-run-after-100-loss-seasons" >White Sox fans are ‘all in’ on long postseason run after 100-loss seasons</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/29/chicago-white-sox-letter-from-pope-leo-postseason-playoffs-houston-astros" >White Sox receive letter from their holiest fan, Pope Leo, before postseason opener</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Cubs and Padres — always the bridesmaids — are a fitting wild-card match
entries.summary: <p>SAN DIEGO — The Battle of the Bridesmaids is underway at Petco Park.</p><p>Gazing upon the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> and Padres as they prepared to get down to business in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/29/cubs-craig-counsell-playoffs-mlb-postseason-game-2-starter-kevin-gausman-shota-imanaga-padres-alex-bregman-playoff-roster" target="_blank" >Game 1 of their National League wild-card series</a>, it occurred to a visitor just how alike these teams are.</p><p>They might be the only two teams in the major leagues that are (1) talented enough to win the World Series, (2) capable of spending what they have to in order to win big and yet (3) are roadblocked, year after year, by the same division bullies they just can’t overcome.</p><p>The Cubs have the Brewers, of course, who have won the NL Central six times since the Cubs last did it in a non-pandemic season (2017). In 2023, the Brewers finished nine games in front of the Cubs, who missed the playoffs by a whisker and fired manager David Ross before pilfering Craig Counsell from their I-94 enemies. Naturally, in 2024, Counsell’s Cubs promptly finished 10 back of Pat Murphy’s Brewers and missed the playoffs again. Last season, the Brewers punctuated yet another division win by knocking the Cubs out of the playoff party, and this year? A 14-game canyon between the Brewers and the second-place Cubs stretched as far as the eye could see.</p><p>The Padres only wish they had a small-market overachiever atop their list of problems. Instead, they have the singular colossus that is the Dodgers, who have claimed 13 of the last 14 NL West titles (and won 106 games in the year they finished second, 2021, the Giants edging them with 107). Still in robust position to contend, the Padres are in the playoffs for the fifth time in the last seven years, having finished second to the Dodgers every one of those times.</p><p>While their tormentors luxuriate, watching wild-card games on television with their feet up and umbrella drinks balanced on their sated bellies, the Cubs and Padres have no choice but to slug it out in a best-of-three series that only makes it harder to achieve Fall Classic dreams.</p><p>“There’s all different paths,” longtime Padres president of baseball operations A.J. Preller said. “We’ve seen teams that have gotten to the World Series by being the hot team going through the wild-card route, and we’ve seen with [other] teams that, obviously, playing one less series can definitely help you.”</p><p>The Brewers — who await the winner of this series — were noticeably fresher last October in the divisional round against the Cubs, who were on fumes after outlasting the Padres in three wild-card games at Wrigley Field.</p><p>Some wild-card teams get hotter than a San Diego tamale and win the whole shebang anyway. But the very idea of the Cubs or Padres potentially getting through both the Brewers and the Dodgers in the coming weeks is a lot to take in.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="113" height="200" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/7Y62_NnBZwo?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="The Sun-Times' Vinnie Duber and Steve Greenberg preview the Cubs-Padres wild card series"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>“I think it forces you to set high standards and play at a high level,” Preller said. “There are challenges, but I think there are also things that you benefit from in terms of being ready for a season and for a postseason. Hopefully, we’re ready for this one.”</p><p>Like the Cubs, who have had a stellar season at the plate and on defense, the Padres have reasons to like their chances and zero room for excuses. From July 24 on, the Padres had the best record in the majors at 41-18. They have the wickedest bullpen in the sport, hands down, and — try to wrap your minds around this — went all-in to the tune of $970 million on the contracts of third baseman Manny Machado, right fielder Fernando Tatis Jr. and shortstop Xander Bogaerts.</p><p>When you throw that much at trying to get past the Dodgers and win all the marbles, it’s no wonder you’ve run through managers as quickly as the Padres have of late, from Jayce Tingler to Bob Melvin to Mike Shildt and now Craig Stammen.</p><p>That’s another thing these two teams have in common — dueling Craigs.</p><p>Cubs skipper Craig Counsell didn’t come here to offer any excuses, not even after his travel-weary team’s odyssey through Boston and St. Petersburg, Florida, on the way here.</p><p>“No repercussions in any way,” Counsell said a few hours before the start of a playoff journey that might last a while, unless it’s over in a jiffy. “We’re ready to go. Sunny San Diego, you know? You can’t beat it. It’s never a bad thing coming here.”</p><p>That’s true. Sometimes, though, it’s a whole lot better to be in a comfy chair with a cold drink, resting up for a series to come.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/29/cubs-playoff-roster-wild-card-series-padres" >Cubs playoff roster set for opening-round series vs. Padres</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/29/cubs-craig-counsell-playoffs-mlb-postseason-game-2-starter-kevin-gausman-shota-imanaga-padres-alex-bregman-playoff-roster" >Craig Counsell and his out-getters aren’t Chicago’s hottest new band, but Cubs’ postseason pitching mantra</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/29/cubs-jed-hoyer-craig-counsell-playoffs-mlb-postseason-world-series" target="_blank" >After work to build, guide Cubs, October is where legacies will be made for Jed Hoyer, Craig Counsell</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Craig Counsell and his out-getters aren't Chicago’s hottest new band, but Cubs’ postseason pitching mantra
entries.summary: <p>SAN DIEGO — <b>Craig Counsell </b>and his out-getters.</p><p>New band name, I call it.</p><p>This is October, when teams and managers start using their pitchers differently than they did all summer long.</p><p>For Counsell and the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a>, that means forgetting who’s a starter and who’s a reliever and who’s supposed to pitch in which inning.</p><p>It’s all about the out-getters.</p><p>‘‘There’s a rhythm to [the regular season]. There’s a rhythm to how players get used. There’s a rhythm to how everything is done,’’ Counsell said Monday. ‘‘Then you turn the calendar to [the playoffs], and everything is done with the utmost urgency.</p><p>‘‘It just matters that we win. That’s the bottom line because we’ve got to win two games in the next three days, so everything — how anybody does, how anything happens — it doesn’t matter. You’ve got to win the game.</p><p>‘‘We’ve just got to figure out how to get 27 outs, and the order that that happens? Starter, reliever, closer, setup man — those words don’t matter.”</p><p>The Cubs opted against naming a starting pitcher for Game 2 of their best-of-three wild-card series against the Padres. That’s unsurprising, considering how Counsell and the team operate: They choose to keep all options on the table.</p><p>Right-hander<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/27/cubs-kevin-gausman-shoulder-injury-game-1-starter-playoffs-wild-card-series-padres-alex-bregman-third-base-pete-crow-armstrong-games-played-start-times" target="_blank" ><b>Kevin Gausman</b>’s left shoulder</a> might affect that decision, though Counsell said Monday that Gausman will pitch in the series. He said the same about left-hander <b>Shota Imanaga</b>, who threw only 12 pitches Sunday.</p><p>It could be anyone and everyone with the stakes this high.</p><p>‘‘This is the playoffs,’’ Counsell said Tuesday. “Everybody just wants to contribute in the playoffs and do whatever they can to help you get a win, help you get to the next round.</p><p>‘‘The buy-in on that, it’s easy. You don’t have to ask for that. They want to do that.’’</p><h3>The ‘uplifting’ Bregman</h3><p>Third baseman <b>Alex Bregman</b>, a little more than a week after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/23/cubs-alex-bregman-face-injury-return-matt-shaw-bunt-daniel-palencia-stats" target="_blank" >taking a foul ball to the face</a> and suffering facial fractures, made it to the postseason.</p><p>‘‘It’s hard to imagine anything keeping him out of a playoff game,’’ second baseman <b>Nico Hoerner</b> said. ‘‘But you start having a broken face, and that definitely would creep into the thoughts of, ‘This might be [the thing].’ ’’</p><p>But no. Bregman wowed — and simultaneously didn’t surprise — his teammates by returning to action just a few days later and then homering twice Sunday.</p><p>‘‘It was super-uplifting just seeing him on the field at all in Boston, just that he seemed to see the ball and took strong swings,’’ Hoerner said. ‘‘Then to do what he did on Sunday was pretty remarkable. Just his attitude within hours of being hit in the face, how quickly he reoriented everything to being ready for the playoffs. Every decision he made worked backwards from that.’’</p><p>Counsell chose to use Bregman as his designate hitter in Game 1, rather than play him at third base.</p><p>‘‘I played it safe, I’ll be honest with you,’’ Counsell said. ‘‘This is a man seven days off of facial fractures. His at-bats are the most critical thing for our team, that he gets his at-bats this series. This is a better way to guarantee that he gets these at-bats.’’</p><h3>Roster choices</h3><p>There wasn’t much drama involving <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/29/cubs-playoff-roster-wild-card-series-padres" target="_blank" >the Cubs’ playoff roster</a>,, but the team kept veteran left-handed reliever <b>Caleb Thielbar </b>off its 26-man group for the series after he finished the regular season with a 4.68 ERA and 11 home runs allowed.</p><p>With Bregman DH’ing, the Cubs also put rarely used infielder <b>Gabriel Arias</b> on the roster to provide depth.</p>

entries.title: White Sox hold on for 6-3 victory over Astros in Game 1 of wild card series
entries.summary: <p>HOUSTON — In terms of rested and reliable starters, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> and Astros were in a similar place on Tuesday evening.</p><p>But the Sox’ Game 1 playoff bullpen game effort was lined up days in advance, and the Astros’ was the leftovers of an all-hands-on-deck effort to clinch a playoff spot on the last day of the season. For most of the Sox’ 6-3 victory, each side looked their respective part.</p><p>A less-than-capacity crowd at Daikin Park, trained on high-quality baseball for the last decade, starting letting boos loose early, as the Sox out-hit the Astros 11-6 in a game they kept stopping just shy of breaking open, but never allowed to grow closer than arm’s length.</p><p>Grant Taylor freezing Astros catcher Yainer Diaz with a full-count curveball to strand two runners ended Houston’s biggest, latest threat in the eighth. Jeremy Pena and Yordan Alvarez, otherwise held in check, hit back-to-back one-out singles, before Miguel Vargas’ throw on a Jose Altuve grounder dragged Munetaka Murakami off the first-base bag.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="113" height="200" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/JFgbsGk2se8?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="White Sox pitcher Grant Taylor talks about the Game 1 win"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>While rookie Hagen Smith glided through three scoreless innings to open the game, his counterpart AJ Blubaugh didn’t throw enough strikes to get out of the first. Bryan King relieved him and limited the damage to a Murakami sacrifice fly. But other than being left-handed and healthy, the strengths to King’s 2026 season are less clear, and Sox left-handed bats handled him fine. After King plunked Colson Montgomery to load the bases, Sam Antonacci lined a two-run single to left-center, before Kyle Teel reloaded them with his own knock.</p><p>Rookie right-hander Miguel Ullola was the unexpected stabilizing force for the Astros pitching staff, striking out Murakami and Andrew Benintendi to escape a bases loaded jam in the second, en route to three innings of work marred only by a Colson Montgomery solo shot. With the close to 2026 that Montgomery endured, sending an 0-2 pitch 432-feet out to dead center looked like an unburdening.</p><p>With another unproven Astros lefty in Josh Hendrickson on in the fifth, Isaac Paredes whiffed on a bases loaded Chase Meidroth bouncer for a run-scoring infield single to put the Sox up 5-0. Still, a Colson Montgomery double play ball ended the frame with no further damage, such that when Nelson Velazquez launched an 0-2 Sean Newcomb fastball over the Crawford Boxes for a pinch-hit two-run shot, the Astros were back in business.</p><p>Former White Sox lefty Bennett Sousa yielded another tally in the seventh, when one of several bounced sliders snuck past Diaz to plate Murakami, who had the first of a pair of singles to lead off the inning. Whereas 6-2 isn’t a save situation in the regular season, in a best-of-three elimination environment, it’s close enough that a runner in scoring position against David Sandlin prompted Will Venable to ask Taylor for seven laborious outs to take things home.</p><p>One idea behind the aggressive move is that while Taylor is shutting things down, the Sox bats have the chance to lengthen the lead enough to allow a less essential reliever to finish things out. That didn’t happen, but the other idea behind it is when a win is in sight a best-of-three playoff series, there are no half-measures.</p><p></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/29/chicago-white-sox-mlb-playoffs-postseason-houston-astros-wild-card-chris-getz-miguel-vargas-chase-meidroth-kyle-teel-colson-montgomery" >Whatever happens, White Sox in better shape than after their last playoff series vs. Astros</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Facing elimination, Cubs starting playoff-tested Kevin Gausman in Game 2 vs. Padres
entries.summary: <p>SAN DIEGO – With their season on the line, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> are turning to the guy who pitched in the World Series last fall.</p><p>Kevin Gausman will get the ball in Game 2 on Wednesday night, announced as the Cubs’ starting pitcher after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/29/cubs-padres-game-1-loss-matthew-boyd-home-runs-fernando-tatis-manny-machado-playoffs-mlb-postseason-wild-card-series" >an ugly 8-0 loss</a> in the first contest of their best-of-three playoff series against the Padres.</p><p>Gausman was the headlining acquisition of the Cubs’ trade-deadline haul, arriving in a win-now deal with a mile-long track record of major league success and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/08/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-kevin-gausman-clay-holmes-world-series-blue-jays-yankees-dodgers" >recent experience pitching under baseball’s brightest lights</a>. He pitched in six playoff games for the Blue Jays last postseason, including making two starts in the World Series.</p><p>After he <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/23/cubs-magic-number-playoffs-clinch-nl-wild-card-standings-kevin-gausman-shoulder-injury" >banged his left shoulder</a> while making a diving tag play in the final week of the regular season, his ability to pitch in this opening-round series has been a hot topic. But manager Craig Counsell said Monday that Gausman would pitch, in some fashion, in the series and announced the righty as the Game 2 starter Tuesday night.</p><p>In the week since he departed a game against the Marlins with the injury, Gausman has been open about his uncertainty that his shoulder would be in good enough shape for him to pitch, and his honest uncertainty about how things will go carried over into the night before his next playoff outing.</p><p>“We’re going to find out,” he said after Tuesday's game, asked how his shoulder was feeling. “It feels all right, good enough to go out there and give it everything I’ve got. That’s what I’m going to do.</p><p>“I’ve had shoulder injuries before, but it’s always been the right one. This one’s been a little bit different. I’ve been trying to feel out the movements and what I’m, maybe, going to have to change a little bit out there to be able to do what I want to do.</p><p>“I feel good enough to go out there. I don’t know if I felt this way a couple days ago.”</p><p>In addition to his questionable health over the last week, Gausman has spent his time in a Cubs uniform bouncing back and forth between terrific starts and subpar ones. He posted a 4.83 ERA in nine regular-season outings for the Cubs, allowing 10 earned runs in 15 1/3 innings across his last three trips to the mound.</p><p>He’ll face the challenge of a red-hot Padres lineup that hit three homers off lefty Matthew Boyd on Tuesday night and sent the Cubs to a blowout defeat.</p><p>His playoff experience has been lauded since he joined the team in August, but Gausman – who was acquired to pitch in moments like these – has just one shot to keep the Cubs’ season alive Wednesday.</p><p>“You try to treat it like a normal game,” he said. “You really can’t when they’re waving towels out there. But you try to stay in the moment and trust yourself and trust the team behind you.”</p>

entries.title: White Sox fans are 'all in' on long playoff run after 100-loss seasons
entries.summary: <p>Eager White Sox fans gathered Tuesday at Cork & Kerry at The Park in Armour Square in anticipation of the team’s first playoff game in five years.</p><p>“I am absolutely sick to my stomach right now, but in a good way,” said Patrick Ramos, before the Sox’ 6-3 victory against the Houston Astros in Game 1 of their American League Wild Card Series.</p><p>Sox fandom is united behind a group of young, fun-loving players, including rookie slugger Munetaka Murakami (the ‘‘South Side Samurai"), who show their personalities on and off the field. They have produced an odds-defying turnaround from the dark days of 2024, when the Sox set a major league record by losing 121 games, and ticket prices dropped to $1.</p><p>Fans are expecting a win and hope to welcome playoff baseball back to the South Side. All three wild-card games are in Houston; the Sox must advance to the next round to play on their home turf.</p><p>“I can't wait for the crowd to be just as insane as when we were going to the World Series, as when we had the blackout game,” said Chris Ramos, Patrick Ramos’ brother, referring to the one-game tiebreaker for a playoff spot the Sox won against the Minnesota Twins in 2008. “I expect that level of intensity in that park when we come back after we win this series.”</p><p>And perhaps the team’s most famous fan is hoping for a successful postseason. Pope Leo XIV, a lifelong Sox fan, penned a letter to the team. It arrived at Rate Field this week.</p><p>“As I have noted, ‘sport can truly become a school of life, where all can learn that abundance does not come from victory at any cost, but from sharing, from respecting others and from the joy of walking together.’ In this spirit, it is my hope that the White Sox will continue to foster bonds of friendship and solidarity among people, and thus bear hopeful witness to the possibility of living and working together in peace,” the pope wrote. “With these sentiments, I willingly invoke the Almighty’s abundant blessings upon you and your loved ones.”</p><div entries.title: Serving up homers and managing only three hits, Cubs on brink of elimination after Game 1 loss to Padres
entries.summary: <p>SAN DIEGO — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> are hoping for a run deep into October.</p><p>But after opening their best-of-three series against the Padres with a multi-faceted thud, they’re in danger of not even reaching Oct. 1.</p><p>The Cubs, who scored more runs than any team in baseball during the regular season, managed only three hits in an 8-0 loss to the Padres on Tuesday night that put them on the brink of elimination.</p><p>But that wasn’t all that went wrong, with lefty Matthew Boyd tagged for three home runs and even the Cubs’ best-in-baseball defense having issues as the Padres poured it on late.</p><p>It was a shockingly poor showing from a team with championship-level expectations, though there was nothing surprising about what a red-hot Padres team and its biggest stars did early.</p><p>Fernando Tatis Jr. and Manny Machado teamed to hit two homers off Boyd in the first inning, their fly balls to center field evading the leaping efforts of Pete Crow-Armstrong and sending Petco Park into a frenzy.</p><p>That duo produced another run off Boyd, on a two-out double, in the third inning before Xander Bogaerts made it three homers off the Cubs’ lefty starter an inning later. A two-run, bases-loaded hit off Ryan Rolison and a passed ball through Carson Kelly’s legs made it 7-0 in the fifth.</p><p>Kelly made another miscue in the seventh, his throwing error on a Tatis stolen base allowing the Padres star to score.</p><p>Boyd had only allowed multiple home runs in three of his 22 starts during the regular season, but one of those games came against these Padres, on June 30, when he gave up home runs to Tatis and Machado.</p><p>But as the night wore on, the story shifted from the Cubs’ pitching woes to center on their inability to do anything offensively.</p><p>Padres starter Michael King took a no-hit bid into the seventh inning, broken up on Nico Hoerner’s infield single. Seiya Suzuki and Hoerner singled in the ninth.</p><p>And that was it.</p><p>It was an offensive performance reminiscent of last week, when the Cubs’ bats struggled to score in cold, windy conditions at Wrigley Field and Fenway Park before scoring a half dozen times in their relocated regular-season finale in Florida.</p><p>They had no such weather-related excuses this time, playing under clear Southern California skies, but the trend continued. They’ve scored just 15 runs in their last seven games, averaging just a hair above two runs per contest.</p><p>That’s not likely to be enough to get the job done in Game 2 against this hot-hitting Padres squad, and the Cubs will have to fix what ails them in a hurry if they’re going to be playing past Wednesday night.</p>

entries.title: Padres' superstars show Cubs how it's done in Game 1 rout
entries.summary: <p>SAN DIEGO — Are you freaking out yet, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> fans?</p><p>Because that was $970 million worth of superstar that took starting pitcher Matthew Boyd over the outfield wall in Game 1 of the wild-card playoffs, an 8-0 romp that made this best-of-three series seem, at least at the outset, like no series at all.</p><p>Fernando Tatis Jr. homered on Boyd’s very first pitch, center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong reaching his glove as high as he could at the fence to no avail. Just like that, a gauntlet was thrown down by a man with a $340 million contract and offensive numbers that, for the last four months, have been right there with those of the soon-to-be National League MVP.</p><p>“Start a game, being at home and hitting a first-pitch home run like that, it just gets everybody going and it brings more energy to the boys,” Tatis said. “And that’s what it’s all about.”</p><p>Two batters later, still in the first inning, Manny Machado took Boyd not so gently into the good night. Ding, ding, ring up another $350 million.</p><p>“We’re always ready for the battle,” Machado said. “This group is ready for the battle through thick and thin.”</p><p>And before Boyd’s regrettable night was through, Xander Bogaerts tagged him, too, into the second deck down the line in left. Let’s see, what’s left from 970? Ah, yes, a player the Padres invested merely $280 million in — even this one, nearly $100 more than the highest-price-tag Cubs contract ever, which still belongs to Jason Heyward — made it a mega-money triple shot of “Our best is a hell of a lot better than yours.”</p><p>Let’s not kid ourselves — this was quite a jolt.</p><p>Scary. Intimidating.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="es" dir="ltr">🔥 ¡BACK TO BACK DE TATIS JR. Y MACHADO!<br><br>Fernando Tatis Jr. sacó el primer picheo del partido y en el turno siguiente Manny Machado hizo lo propio para ponerle otra rayita a Padres en la alta de la primera entrada vs Cubs.<br><br>📹: MLB<a href="https://x.com/hashtag/MLBxESPN?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#MLBxESPN</a> <a href="https://t.co/VgdInZXyv2">pic.twitter.com/VgdInZXyv2</a></p>— ESPN.com.do🇩🇴 (@ESPN_DO) <a href="https://x.com/ESPN_DO/status/2105122045960847761?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 30, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Who’s betting on the Cubs to win Games 2 and 3 against the hottest team in baseball over the last two-plus months — which happens to be the hottest it has been right now, with 18 wins in its last 21 games counting Tuesday?</p><p>Any takers? Any at all?</p><p>All three Padres stars had multiple hits, which is more than could be said about the entire Cubs team until the ninth inning. Michael King sliced and diced Cubs hitters for seven one-hit innings, the only blemish coming on an infield dribbler off the bat of Nico Hoerner. If King isn’t a straight-up ace, he sure looked like one. The Cubs no doubt had a hand in creating the impression.</p><p>It wasn’t just the Cubs’ hitting stars — namely Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman — who failed to ring the bell, but rather the entire lineup. We are left to wonder if a much-ballyhooed lineup that struggled down the stretch is really anything special at all.</p><p>Not that the Cubs’ pitching situation is any easier to lean on. It isn’t.</p><p>Trouble has arrived.</p><p>The Padres’ superstars made sure of it.</p><p>“They energized the entire stadium,” second baseman Jake Cronensworth said. “Those guys go, we go.”</p><p>“You just follow your leaders,” center fielder Jackson Merrill said. “That’s how we roll.”</p><p>Perhaps Crow-Armstrong and Bregman will return the favor in Game 2 and turn this into a series after all. Wouldn’t that be nice?</p><p>But the Padres are on fire. They’re busting at the seams with confidence. They have all the momentum and mojo in the world — and, apparently, all the money.</p><p>"Well, that's not how you draw it up," Cubs chairman Tom Ricketts deadpanned as he stepped onto a crowded elevator after the game.</p><p>The giant money talked when it mattered most.</p><p>All the Cubs could do was shut up and listen.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/30/cubs-game-2-playoff-starter-starting-pitcher-kevin-gausman-wild-card-series-mlb-postseason" target="_blank" >Facing elimination, Cubs starting playoff-tested Kevin Gausman in Game 2 vs. Padres</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/30/cubs-playoffs-game-1-game-2-wild-card-series-padres-alex-bregman-matthew-boyd-carson-kelly" target="_blank" >Cubs look to summon much-discussed resilience to extend season past Wednesday: ‘It’s what we’re made of’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Cubs look to summon much-discussed resilience to extend season past Wednesday: ‘It’s what we’re made of’
entries.summary: <p>SAN DIEGO – Before the month of October has even arrived, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> are faced with an early playoff elimination.</p><p>Game 1 of their best-of-three series against the Padres on Tuesday night went all kinds of wrong, with lefty starter Matthew Boyd serving up three homers, the highest scoring lineup in baseball held to just three hits and even an all-time great defense struggling, at points.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/29/cubs-padres-game-1-loss-matthew-boyd-home-runs-fernando-tatis-manny-machado-playoffs-mlb-postseason-wild-card-series" >An 8-0 defeat</a> was not what a team with World Series aspirations had in mind. It’s not what anyone expected to see.</p><p>And it’s something that could help end this postseason run before it even gets going.</p><p>“We didn’t do anything right today,” third baseman Alex Bregman said. “We’ve got to execute better in all phases of the game.</p><p>“You flush it, turn the page. You’ve got to this time of year. I’ve got all the confidence in the world this group can bounce back tomorrow.”</p><p>The Cubs spent the summer describing their ability to reset after the emotional highs and lows of wins and losses. They spent the last week, with more challenges thrown their way, talking about all they’ve weathered this season.</p><p>They’ve got one chance Wednesday to prove that resilience is the defining feature they believe it to be and keep their season going another night.</p><p>“It’s what we’re made of. We’re able to do that,” Boyd said. “We’ve got a lot of fight in this clubhouse. We’ll come out here, we’ll leave this one behind and be ready to do a job tomorrow. … We believe in our group, and we’re never out of it.”</p><p>“This one leaves a little sour taste in your mouth,” catcher Carson Kelly said, “but I have this saying: We shower well. Once you go take a shower, it’s over, and you move to the next day. That’s what we’re going to do.”</p><p>The Cubs could arrive at Petco Park with that perfect mindset, but it’ll need to carry over into the game. If they look like they did Tuesday, the only place they’ll be advancing is the couch.</p><p>Tuesday was all sorts of ugly, with the hot-hitting Padres bashing Boyd early, superstars Fernando Tatis Jr. and Manny Machado homering off him in the first inning. Xander Bogaerts added to the barrage a few innings later.</p><p>The bullpen didn’t exactly shine, either, giving up four runs of their own, though two came on rare defensive mistakes, with Kelly letting a passed ball get between his legs and making a throwing error on a stolen-base try that allowed Tatis to score.</p><p>Meanwhile, the Cubs were hitless after six innings, mustering only one knock – an infield single – off Padres starter Michael King before loading the bases with two more hits in the ninth. The team’s two biggest offensive stars, center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong and Bregman, combined to strike out six times in eight trips to the plate.</p><p>None of it looked championship-caliber in the least, especially when compared to a scorching Padres team that seemingly did everything right and had their home fans going crazy.</p><p>It leaves the Cubs with some fixes to make in a hurry. In the no-margin-for-error world of playoff baseball, it’s make those fixes or call it a season.</p><p>“You’ve got no choice but to [turn the page],” Bregman said. “Then you come the next day and you compete your tail off and lay it all out there.”</p><p>“Luckily, we’re living tomorrow,” Boyd said. “We’ll come back punching tomorrow.”</p>

entries.title: Blackhawks' defense shredded by Golden Knights in season-opening loss
entries.summary: <p>LAS VEGAS — The Blackhawks' popularity worked against them for scheduling purposes yet again this year, with the NHL handing them a brutal road trip to start the season.</p><p>A stacked, motivated Golden Knights team gave the Hawks very little opportunity to ease into the regular season Tuesday. But the Hawks also gave the Knights very little difficulty in a 5-2 loss.</p><p>For the Hawks, the good news was they improved in each period. The bad news was they went from awful to bad to OK.</p><p>"We shouldn’t be satisfied with the level of game we had tonight, because I don’t think it was nearly our A-game," coach Jeff Blashill said.</p><p>Said new defenseman Bowen Byram: "I just think we weren't necessarily dialed in on what we had to do, and it showed right in the first...30 to 45 minutes of the game."</p><p>One noticeable part of the Knights' game plan — cheating for transition offense — relied upon the assumption that the Hawks usually wouldn't be able to make plays to catch the Knights outnumbered down low. And that assumption generally proved correct.</p><p>The Hawks struggled to defend those Knights' transition attacks, too. The gaps from their defensemen weren't consistently tight, and their forwards were often caught chasing.</p><p>"I didn’t think we were very good in the first," coach Jeff Blashill. "[We were] really shaky with the puck. We just didn’t execute and make crisp, clean plays. We'd break into the zone and kind of give it away, and that puts you on your heels if you’re turning pucks over in those areas like we did.</p><p>"Against that team, if you’re a defenseman, you either have to be right down on the puck down the walls, or you have to be inside the dots. If you’re in between at all, which we were a couple of times, they fly out of the zone and it’s going to be a two-on-one instantaneously."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Knights goal: Noah Hanifin beats Knight five hole. <a href="https://t.co/1EnMihVjkT">pic.twitter.com/1EnMihVjkT</a></p>— BHF (@BlackhawksFocus) <a href="https://x.com/BlackhawksFocus/status/2105157802813784348?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 30, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Offensively, the Hawks should also be a decent rush team themselves this season, and they showed some flashes of that. Patrick Kane scored a pretty breakaway goal — in his first game back with the Hawks — to briefly cut the deficit to 3-2 in the third period.</p><p>But in general, the transition offense wasn't as dangerous as the transition defense was vulnerable.</p><p>"You don’t want to be turning over the puck, feeding the rush game the other way," Kane said. "Obviously we want to be an aggressive team on the puck. ... We [will] watch the video, learn from our mistakes and go from there. It’s on everyone."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Yeah, Patrick Kane is still Patrick Kane <a href="https://t.co/BFS3GmEhI6">pic.twitter.com/BFS3GmEhI6</a></p>— Ben Pope (@BenPopeCST) <a href="https://x.com/BenPopeCST/status/2105157774963605800?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 30, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>It will take more than one road game against an elite opponent to thorough assess the supposedly new-and-improved 2026-27 Hawks. The fact they lost Tuesday wasn't surprising.</p><p>More concerning was how, after an offseason of emphasizing puck possession, the only Hawks line able to sustain much possession — at least before score effects took hold in the third period — was Ryan Greene and Jordan Greenway's fourth line.</p><p>The other three lines that Blashill shuffled in practice Monday all struggled to varying degrees. The Hawks also lost Andrew Mangiapane to a lower-body injury that will sideline him for the next two games at minimum.</p><p>Before the game, general manager Kyle Davidson preached patience with the experiment of deploying rookies Anton Frondell and Roman Kantserov at center, since it will take them time to get their bearings in the NHL. </p><p>"That's not an easy position to play, much like defense in the NHL," Davidson said. "I'm sure there's going to be some growing pains, but we're walking in knowing that. [We have] a lot of confidence that their hockey sense and talent will carry them through."</p><p>Hawks fans are understandably tired of being patient, though, whether or not it's prudent. After this trip, they'll deserve some things to celebrate during the rest of the October schedule, which is loaded with home games.</p><p>The Hawks don't have long to find their sea legs before then.</p>

entries.title: Motorist was intoxicated during fatal wrong way wreck on South DuSable Lake Shore Drive, police say
entries.summary: <p>A man was charged with a fatal wrong way crash that left a woman dead Sunday night on South DuSable Lake Shore Drive. </p><p>Faymond Johnson, 33, was charged with aggravated DUI resulting in accidental death, reckless homicide with a motor vehicle driving under the influence of alcohol, Chicago police said. </p><p>Johnson, of North Lawndale, was arrested less than an hour after police identified him as the person who was driving a black SUV on the wrong side of the drive when he struck a white sedan head-on in the 4000 block of South DuSable Lake Shore Drive, causing a chain-reaction crash, police said. </p><p>A 35-year-old woman driving white sedan, Yoketha Brown, 35, died at Northwestern Memorial Hospital, police said.</p><p>Johnson was scheduled for a detention hearing at the Leighton Criminal Courthouse Wednesday. </p>

entries.title: Corporate fund’s structural deficit — not Brandon Johnson — to blame for city's financial woes
entries.summary: <p>Chicago’s political season is hitting full swing, with the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/09/13/chicago-mayor-brandon-johnson-announcement-reelection-bid-2027" >mayor’s office</a>, as well as all 50 aldermanic seats, up for election. This means the airwaves will be inundated with charged rhetoric, hyperbole and the all-time favorite political activity: finger-pointing. Amid that cacophony, Mayor Brandon Johnson will be introducing his fourth corporate fund budget proposal for the city.</p><p>That’s vitally important because the corporate fund is Chicago’s primary operating budget. It covers the core public services residents expect city government to provide, including everything from police and fire protection, to streets and sanitation services, healthcare and social services. Fiscal difficulties in the corporate fund translate into inadequate service levels, which in turn translate into unhappy residents and a lower quality of life. Unfortunately, for over a decade and through numerous different mayoral administrations, city decision makers have struggled to cobble together a balanced budget for the corporate fund.</p><p>For instance, when the current $6.25 billion corporate fund budget was being negotiated, the fund faced a deficit of just under $1.2 billion, or 18.8%. To be clear, that meant Chicago didn’t have 18.8% of the money needed to continue providing the same level of public services it delivered during the prior year. Ultimately, most of that deficit was eliminated through a series of actions that included everything from spending cuts, to generating both recurring revenue through increased taxes and fees and one-time revenue through the declaration of a record $1 billion tax increment financing surplus, the sale of some city assets and the issuance of $166 million in debt. However, all one-time revenue that funds ongoing operations has to be replaced with new dollars in subsequent years to maintain service levels. Oh, and the debt has to be repaid, with interest, creating even more fiscal stress as time passes.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c20000" name="module-c20000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>So it shouldn’t shock anyone that in the coming fiscal year, the corporate fund again faces a significant, $882.4 million deficit to fill. It also shouldn’t be surprising that the blame game has already begun. Indeed, it seems everyone with a horse in the mayoral race wants to lay culpability for Chicago’s fiscal woes at Johnson's feet. But doing so is both inaccurate and counterproductive.</p><p>It’s inaccurate because all the evidence shows the recurring budget gaps in the corporate fund are not attributable to poor management decisions made by the current or any of the immediately preceding, mayoral administrations. Instead, they’re the predictable consequence of the corporate fund’s structural deficit. A “structural deficit” exists whenever a government’s revenue is projected to grow at a rate that’s insufficient to both continue funding the same level of public services from year to year, adjusting solely for inflation and pay existing debt service obligations as they become due.</p><p>That’s precisely the predicament facing the corporate fund. In fact, over one-third of the corporate fund’s existing revenue sources are incapable of growing with the economy over time, even though the cost of funding services does. Meanwhile state law historically created a pension-funding matrix that allowed Chicago to underfund its pension systems. This effectively let the city use revenue that should’ve funded pensions to instead cover service delivery costs. The net result: For decades Chicagoans consumed public services without having to pay the full cost thereof in taxes, and the city racked up a ton of debt to its pensions.</p><p>That practice was ended in 2010, when state legislation created a back-loaded amortization schedule that imposes annually increasing contributions on Chicago to repay the substantial pension debt it incurred. When you couple a back-loaded debt repayment plan with a revenue system that doesn’t grow with the economy, you get a textbook structural deficit.</p><p>It’s counterproductive for politicians to waste the public’s time playing the budget blame game, because Chicago’s long-term, structural fiscal problems can only be redressed through long-term, structural reforms. Those reforms are politically difficult to champion. Hence the finger-pointing, which allows candidates to avoid offering real, sustainable solutions, which is hard, and instead pander to voters, which is easy.</p><p>A classic example of such counterproductive pandering is the tired, yet oft repeated pledge to not increase property taxes. Sure, everyone hates property taxes, but think about it: corporate fund revenue doesn’t grow with the economy, thereby diminishing Chicago’s capacity to maintain service levels over time. The property tax is the largest revenue source available to Chicago, clocking in at $1.8 billion this year. The vast majority of those dollars cover Chicago’s pension contribution, which will total over $2.94 billion next year, when the advance pension payment is added to the required payment under the back-loaded amortization schedule. Not increasing property taxes would effectively force Chicago to divert even more corporate fund revenue to cover its pension debt — further constraining the city’s capacity to fund core services. That’s not solving problems — it’s making them worse.</p><p><i>Ralph Martire is executive director of the Center for Tax and Budget Accountability, a nonpartisan fiscal policy think tank, and the Arthur Rubloff professor of public policy at Roosevelt University.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-090000" name="module-090000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: I got my doctorate at 75, which shows it's never too late to pursue your dream
entries.summary: <p>A recent report by the Council for Adult and Experiential Learning revealed <a class="Link" href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/michaeltnietzel/2026/06/11/over-41-million-adults-say-they-want-to-enroll-in-college-but-will-they/" target="_blank" >more than 41 million American adults</a> intend to go back to school or into a training program within the next two years. Many of those people are older adults, and researchers call us the <a class="Link" href="https://fortune.com/2026/02/22/older-adults-continuing-education-school-new-majority-student-upskilling-career-change/" target="_blank" >“new majority student.</a>"</p><p>I'm one of those adults. This year, at 75, I got my Ph.D.</p><p>Most headlines about older adults receiving degrees assume we're all chasing bigger paychecks or scrambling to keep up with new technology. Some are. But I didn't go back for a raise or a better title as I retired years ago. I went back because dreams don't come with an expiration date, and I wasn't willing to let mine quietly run out.</p><p>I come from a family that believes in education, and most of my siblings have multiple degrees. I'd always thought about going back to get a Ph.D. in education, and I wasn’t willing to let my age be an excuse to not do it. So I started my doctoral work in 2015.</p><p>It took me 11 years. Along the way, I encountered health challenges that were good enough reasons to quit. There were times I had to step back and take care of myself. But I’m lucky to have blind faith in myself, and I was cheered on by my family and my community at the Chicago Housing Authority's Zelda Ormes Apartments. They supported my insistence on finishing what I had started. That's made the difference between a dream deferred and a dream completed.</p><p>This spring, I defended my dissertation on the importance of teaching Black history to children and received my Ph.D. in education and leadership at DePaul University. I'm now the only one in my family with three degrees — a bachelor's, a master's and a doctorate. I like to remind my nieces, nephews and even great-grand nieces that if I can do it at 75, they have no excuses.</p><p>I'm telling my story because I know many people carry a dream they've quietly decided is too late, too big or too far out of reach. Trust me when I say you don’t have to see the whole staircase to take the first step.</p><p>My neighbors have watched this journey, and I hope watching it gives somebody — perhaps a senior or a young person in another CHA community — the courage to begin their own journey. Go back to school. Start the business. Finish the thing you stepped back from. Going back is what matters.</p><p><i>Deniece Rogers, Chicago Housing Authority resident, Near North Side</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-fe0000" name="module-fe0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Landlords aren’t living large </h3><p>As a mom-and-pop landlord, I see Chicago media coverage and policy as pro-tenant. I understand that history shows those in power taking advantage of those with less power. But through the internet, tenants have gained power through online tenant organizations. Business owners, including landlords, live in fear of negative reviews, viral posts and threats of lawsuits.</p><p>Most landlords are regular people who are trying to earn enough money to retire. My husband and I own two small residences on the North Side. Though we both work full-time jobs, we spend our weekends maintaining the properties. We are not rich, despite what the media coverage would have you think. When everyone stayed home during the pandemic and was using water at home instead of at work all day, we paid for the increase. When labor and materials increase in price because of labor shortages and tariffs, we pay for the increase. When we are hit with higher property taxes, we pay for the increase.</p><p>Now through his Protecting Renters Ordinance, Mayor Brandon Johnson wants to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/16/brandon-johnson-renters-protection-ordinance-aldermen-dueling-proposals-chicago-city-council-housing-committe" >ban move-in fees</a>, the only means landlords have to protect themselves against property damage since security deposits are too much of a lawsuit risk. Mayor, please stop hiding behind your so-called “Tenant Bill of Rights." Everyone sees the ordinance as a means to get reelected with nothing but more costs that landlords will pass on to tenants out of necessity, not greed. Unlike Brandon Johnson, landlords don’t have the option of not paying our <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2024/09/20/unpaid-fines-fees-cta-city-workers-18-million-uncollected-debt" >water bills </a>before getting caught.</p><p><i>Greta Connor, Evanston</i></p><h3>Two styles of postseason bliss</h3><p>My wife compared the photos of the Cubs and Sox teams on the back page of Saturday's Sun-Times.</p><p>The Cubs photo is formal, well-organized, everyone in place, "Clinched" on the scoreboard in the background, the players in front furling "W" flags, fans in the stands in the background.</p><p>The Sox appear a bit more disheveled, a couple of players shirtless, a couple more lying on the ground, many with sunglasses perched on their hats, asymmetrically arranged, a blank scoreboard and empty stands in the background.</p><p>One thing both teams have in common: All appear to be having a very good time, which they all well deserve.</p><p><i>Julius L. "Jerry" Loeser, Lake Forest</i></p><h3><b>Pessimistic predictions help </b></h3><p>Thanks to Sun-Times columnist Steve Greenberg for doing his civic duty by predicting that both the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/27/cubs-padres-white-sox-astros-mlb-playoffs-wild-card-pete-crow-armstrong-petco" target="_blank" ><u>Sox and Cubs</u></a> will lose their first-round playoff series. This negative Nostradamus now has virtually assured us that there will be second round playoff games on both sides of town. A grateful city breathes a little easier.</p><p><i>Jim Bruton, Avondale</i></p><h3>Riding safe on the CTA </h3><p>Kudos to Chicago.</p><p>I rode the CTA's Purple, Red, Green and Blue lines one day last week. Every major station had K-9 police.</p><p>As a senior citizen from the suburbs, I was quite impressed. I felt truly safe.</p><p><i>Randy F. Gollay, Buffalo Grove</i></p><h3>Hypocritical hype</h3><h3></h3><p>So Donald Trump, the president who threatens to <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/at-un-general-assembly-irans-president-responds-to-trumps-annihilation" target="_blank" >annihilate Iran</a>, is re-airing a <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-administration-uses-taxpayer-money-to-air-2024-trump-campaign-ad" target="_blank" >2024 TV ad</a> in which he rants against "warmongers"?</p><p>Talk about ironic! </p><p><i>Dan McGuire, Bensenville</i><br></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Senior discovers beau is cheating with much younger woman
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I'm a senior woman who has been dating someone for three years. He is my age. I recently learned he has been cheating on me with a much younger woman with three kids. We are sexually active and enjoy each other very much, or at least I thought so. She knows about me.</p><p>Although he treats me well, I have found evidence that he's having sex with her intermittently. I have never cheated on him, and I dislike cheaters. He wants to marry me, but I told him when we first met I didn't want to remarry or live with anyone because I've been married twice, and so has he. I really care about this man, and I thought he loved me, but I don't think I can be with a cheater. Should I confront him or leave it alone? I know I'd miss him dearly, as we do everything together. I also don't want to be alone at this time of my life. Please advise what I should do. — <i>MONOGAMOUS IN LOS ANGELES</i></p><p><b>DEAR MONOGAMOUS:</b> You state that you told this man you do not want to remarry or live with him. You have a great relationship, but not once in your letter did you say that you love him. I see no reason why you shouldn't continue enjoying his companionship. Because the cheating bothers you, consider ending the sex and putting him in the friend zone. If you don't, be sure to get tested for sexually transmitted infections regularly.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am a 60-year-old male. In my first marriage, my ex had an affair, and during the last seven years of that marriage, we lived essentially separate lives. It was a lonely time for me. I have since remarried, and my new wife has a large family, including two sets of parents, four kids and 10 grandkids. My family is significantly smaller, with two kids and no grandkids.</p><p>The issue is that my love language is one-on-one quality time. I have asked my wife to set aside some time for us with no family interruptions. I have suggested date nights (a four-hour time slot two nights or afternoons a month) where we would not take calls or texts from family members. She has struggled to commit to this and instead told me I should "just let life happen." She has trouble turning her phone off and said I should trust her to make judgments about whether to take a call or text. I would like to know if my request is unreasonable and how else uninterrupted quality time can be achieved. — <i>MISSOURI HIKER</i></p><p><b>DEAR HIKER:</b> You will never pry that phone out of your wife's hand. She has clearly shown you that her extended family is her top priority, so stop trying to take that away from her. On date nights, choose activities that will keep her busy and engaged. Keep the conversation flowing, and demonstrate that your full attention is on her. Most importantly, it is OK to insist on a "phones off" rule when things become intimate.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>
