entries.title: CPS School Board candidate Sendhil Revuluri drops out, making it a three-way race
entries.summary: <p>One of four remaining candidates for Chicago School Board president is suspending his campaign, saying he’s come to the conclusion that he cannot compete with the special interest groups pouring money into the election.</p><p>Sendhil Revuluri’s name will still be on the Nov. 3 ballot, but he said Tuesday that he’s “not willing to spend either an irresponsible amount of my own money or spend more of others' time, money and energy trying to keep up when these other groups have leaned into messaging that's completely unrelated to student success, but is backed by a lot of resources.”</p><p>“More Chicagoans gave more to this campaign than to any other candidate. It still was not enough to keep pace with the flood of outside money,” said Revuluri, who was trying to return to the board after serving as vice president under former Mayor Lori Lightfoot.</p><p>This is the first time Chicago voters will elect the school board president in a citywide contest, along with 20 members who will represent 20 geographic districts. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/president/" target="_blank" ><u>The president</u></a> is an especially important position because that person is responsible for deciding what items make it onto monthly school board meeting agendas.</p><p>Revuluri is the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-school-board/2026/08/27/jennifer-custer-drops-out-of-race-for-chicago-school-board-president" target="_blank" ><u>second presidential candidate to drop out</u></a>. The remaining candidates are current school board member Jessica Biggs, former Chicago Teachers Union deputy political director Hilario Dominguez and prominent defense attorney Victor Henderson.</p><p>Revuluri, a former math teacher who now works on start-ups and as a leadership consultant, was the first to announce his campaign almost a year ago. He was motivated by the current partly elected, partly appointed board that he said spends a “very small fraction” of time on district goals or academics.</p><p>Revuluri got an early start on fundraising and still has the most money, but the $750,000 in his coffers includes $400,000 that he loaned to his campaign. The second biggest contributor to his campaign is Chicago Democrats for Education, a political action committee launched by heavyweight political consultant Hugo Jacobo during the first school board election in 2024 to support “independent” candidates for the school board.</p><p>But Revuluri said on Tuesday that his support was dwarfed by backing that other candidates have received from labor unions. About $2.2 million have been pumped into the campaign coffers of school board presidential candidates, including the loans from candidates to themselves.</p><p>So far, the Chicago Teachers Union and its related political groups have spent $276,000 on Dominguez, according to Illinois State Board of Elections records. The Service Employees International Union gave Jessica Biggs $160,000 and a related PAC, Brighter Futures, has spent another $237,000 on ads supporting Biggs.</p><p>Once allies, the CTU and SEIU became estranged after CTU organizer Brandon Johnson was elected mayor SEIU Local 73, which represents CPS support staff, accused the CTU of using its newfound power to try to raid its members.</p><p>Revuluri insists this feud has nothing to do with “ensuring student success.” Instead, he said it has become about political vendettas, ideology and drama.</p><p>If he had been elected school board president, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/sendhil-revuluri/" target="_blank" ><u>Revuluri said</u></a> he would have created an evaluation process for the superintendent and tried to hold her accountable for student achievement. He also said he would be open to closing schools, but instead of doing it to save money his focus would be to move students out of very small schools that often lack a variety of classes and programs.</p><p>Revuluri also said he would have tried to confront the school district’s budget reality — a dig at the current board that approved a budget based on uncommitted <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/07/30/chicago-school-board-approves-budget-that-reverses-layoffs-but-counts-on-shaky-state-funds" target="_blank" ><u>city and state funding that may not materialize</u></a>.</p><p>Revuluri said he is not endorsing any of the remaining candidates.</p><p>“I haven't yet seen evidence that Biggs, Henderson or Dominguez have the integrity and courage that's needed to do this job effectively,” he said. Revuluri said he won’t back anyone until he sees “some evidence that they are going to be willing and able to govern effectively for our students' success.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-440000" name="module-440000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>More CPS School Board coverage</b><br><br>WBEZ and the Chicago Sun-Times have created resources to help voters prepare for this fall’s historic Chicago School Board election. (73.7 × 108.6 × 7 cm);Private collection, Illinois;Installation view of Gertrude Abercrombie: The Whole World Is a Mystery, Carnegie Museum of Art, Pittsburgh (January 18, 2025–June 1, 2025);GA.2025.106" srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/de609a7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2400x1347+0+291/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffd%2Fee%2Fbcb1322b451db17f92f8dc1ac3fc%2F2025-01-16-thewholeworldisamystery-103-print-2400px.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8cb15dc/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2400x1347+0+291/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffd%2Fee%2Fbcb1322b451db17f92f8dc1ac3fc%2F2025-01-16-thewholeworldisamystery-103-print-2400px.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/de609a7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2400x1347+0+291/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffd%2Fee%2Fbcb1322b451db17f92f8dc1ac3fc%2F2025-01-16-thewholeworldisamystery-103-print-2400px.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Eric Crosby co-organized a touring Abercrombie retrospective that opened in January 2025 at the Carnegie Museum in Pittsburgh, pictured here. After witnessing the enthusiasm around the exhibit, he is not surprised that the story and sale of “Alderman Merriam’s shells” has generated so much interest.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Zachary Riggleman/Carnegie Museum of Art, Pittsburgh</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“I think Gertrude Abercrombie,” he said, “is quite conscious about the staging of her scenes and the objects she brings into constellation, and each one has the feeling of a musical chord or a tone poem or some other register beyond the visual.”</p><p>When considering the history of 20th Century American art, Crosby said, the focus for too long has been on New York City. But curators are increasingly looking at what was happening elsewhere, especially in Chicago.</p><p>“The unique conditions in Chicago during Gertrude Abercrombie’s time,” he said, “her relationship with other painters, writers and poets and particularly her close relationship with Black jazz musicians created a really fertile artistic context.”</p><p>Crosby witnessed the enthusiasm around the Abercrombie retrospective, so he is not surprised that the story and sale of “Alderman Merriam’s shells” has generated so much interest. “There is something about this artist that people find uniquely fascinating,” he said. “When a new painting is revealed, people are attracted to the news of it. It’s wonderful.”</p>

Actually, I could do more of this.’"</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-350000" name="module-350000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3><b>Audrey Niffenegger talks “Life Out of Order”</b></h3><h4><b>Naperville</b></h4><b>When</b>: Oct. 2 at 7 p.m.<br><b>Where</b>: Wentz Concert Hall (171 E. Wilson Ave.)<br><b>Tickets</b>: $47.73</div> </div><p>Fans of her literary sci-fi romance may soon feel the same about her sequel, “Life Out of Order” (Oct. 6, Harper Collins). Written over a 12-year stretch while Niffenegger was living between London and Chicago, it moves beyond the orbit of the original love story between Claire and Henry into the lives, passions and rebellions of a second generation of time travelers, including their daughter, Alba DeTamble, a violinist.</p><p>Alba’s world is different from her parents. Time traveling is a known condition, and Niffenegger worked to get “the feeling of daily life into that experience.” There are many more and different kinds of relationships, including Alba’s encounters with her own self at different ages.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-290000" name="image-290000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8bfc7da/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd0%2F06%2F703f6a884eb0a0f429cef0179831%2Faudreyniff-261004-9.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6b618a3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd0%2F06%2F703f6a884eb0a0f429cef0179831%2Faudreyniff-261004-9.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/86a9c46/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd0%2F06%2F703f6a884eb0a0f429cef0179831%2Faudreyniff-261004-9.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Author Audrey Niffenegger holds a copy of her new book, Life Out of Order, inside her home in the Irving Park neighborhood of Chicago on Sept. 17, 2026. there are discoveries, revolutions, greets and goodbyes, but not in the order most people would expect.”</p><p>That convoluted reality was the author’s, too.</p><p>“I didn't think I could do another book where it's like, ‘Time travel, isn't this wild?’ because I feel like the readership has grown up and the fandom for things like ‘Doctor Who’ is so huge now,” muses Niffenegger. “Readers have become much more adept at following things that are not in chronological order.”</p><p>Seated at a table in front of a long row of windows in her Victorian-era home, her signature flowing auburn locks now cut fashionably short, Niffenegger notes that she is “not a futurist.”</p><p>Instead, she began building the future by scanning the present. “I started thinking, well, one thing we can depend on is climate change. I'm pretty sure that will be a problem.”</p><p>Other aspects were less predictable, like the book’s political climate. The opening scene at a house party, set in a Chicago under martial law, involves a group of young people, Alba among them, plotting to take out some fascists.</p><p>“I wrote that in 2013 when neo-Nazis were not really a big problem as far as I could tell,” recalls Niffenegger. “The whole return of fascism thing caught me by surprise.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div I think that any time you get preoccupied with time, grief will certainly come into it.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Victor Hilitski for the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>AI is also part of the plot, although Niffenegger imagines it as a machine for preserving rather than usurping human experience. The heart of the novel remains the relationships between people, including between Alba and her two husbands, one of them also a time traveler.</p><p>Combining a multi-generational tale with a multiverse narrative could potentially lead to sprawl, so Niffenegger imposed some strict boundaries, including limiting first-person point of view to Alba’s immediate family members.</p><p>“You always start to have this feeling as a reader of everything's kind of getting a little hard to handle,” she asserts. “I’m thinking of things like ‘War and Peace’ but also something like ‘Game of Thrones.’ I think the reason he [‘Game of Thrones’ author George R. R. Martin] is having a hard time finishing it is he's just got way too many people to deal with.”</p><p>As Niffenegger was building the book’s alternate world, her own life was evolving. Just as she started writing, she met and fell in love with her now husband, comics artist Eddie Campbell. Her father died in 2016, which she says made writing about Alba and Henry’s relationship “a little bit more fraught and poignant.”</p><p>A sense of grief permeates “Life Out of Order,” but this is familiar terrain for Niffenegger.</p><p>“Most of my work over my whole life has had to do with loss and grief and love and sex and death and rock and roll. So none of these things are new for me. I think that any time you get preoccupied with time, grief will certainly come into it.”</p><p>Now that “Life Out of Order”<i> </i>is finished and entering the world, Niffenegger misses what she describes as the “companionship” of the book she spent the last 12 years writing.</p><p>“I feel like I have a radio station in my head, and the characters are free to chime in whenever they want, and I'm just trying to catch whatever wisp of an idea has popped into my head,” she notes. “It feels strange now to get up in the morning and not have that. entries.title: People charged with drug crimes, shoplifting have a new path to avoid a conviction in Cook County
entries.summary: <p>People charged with drug crimes, shoplifting and other nonviolent misdemeanors can now avoid a criminal conviction under a new program being touted by Cook County prosecutors.</p><p>This week, the Cook County state’s attorney’s office will start allowing defendants in certain low-level cases to complete programming in exchange for having their charges dropped.</p><p>“By providing services to address challenges such as substance abuse or mental health, we can make it less likely that these individuals will commit more crimes,” Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke said in a statement. “When appropriate, we can hold people accountable while also giving them a real opportunity to avoid future involvement in the criminal justice system.”</p><p>A form of diversion programming for misdemeanor cases existed prior to the pandemic but fell through the cracks when the courts moved online, according to Emily Cole, who oversees the state’s attorney’s Alternative Prosecution and Sentencing Unit.</p><p>This new iteration, known as the Misdemeanor Deferred Prosecution Program, is reorganized and far more expansive, Cole said.</p><p>“The idea behind diversion, in particular this diversion, is to connect individuals with community services and resources that would address underlying reasons that may have contributed to their criminal conduct,” she said in an interview.</p><p>“You're helping them get connected to address a root cause, as well as holding the individual accountable for their actions and for the crime that they committed.”</p><p>There are three different tracks for deferred prosecution programming.</p><p>The behavioral health courts serve those with mental health conditions, substance abuse issues or housing insecurity. Veteran’s court offers programming to former service members. And the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2022/10/13/23403105/restorative-justice-court-program-graduates-hope-bright-future" target="_blank" >restorative justice courts</a> focus on repairing the harms caused by a specific crime.</p><p>After determining a person's eligibility for one of those tracks, prosecutors must get the victim’s consent to proceed. The person facing charges will then complete an assessment and receive recommendations, along with an order to return to court in 90 days. If the person completes the recommendations by the 90-day deadline, their charges will be dismissed during that hearing.</p><p>The state’s attorney’s office is particularly excited about the possibility of referring more cases to the county’s restorative justice courts. This marks the first time misdemeanor cases will be sent there, the office said. </p><p>“They're currently not as utilized as they could be,” Cole said, “and they offer a lot of resources and connections within the community.”</p><p>Cook County has four <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2020/7/31/21349836/restorative-justice-courts-open-englewood-avondale" target="_blank" >restorative justice courts</a>, based in Englewood, North Lawndale, Avondale and suburban Sauk Village. A person must be between 18 and 24 years old and live in one of those areas to qualify for the programming.</p><p>In addition to the other non-violent offenses, people charged with possession of ammunition and possession of a firearm with an expired gun license will also now be eligible for the restorative justice courts.</p><p>Those who fail to meet program requirements or pick up a new case could still be convicted.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2022/10/13/23403105/restorative-justice-court-program-graduates-hope-bright-future" target="_blank" >Graduates of Restorative Justice Court program hope for a bright future</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2020/7/31/21349836/restorative-justice-courts-open-englewood-avondale" target="_blank" >2 new restorative justice courts to open next month in Avondale and Englewood</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Fall bridge lifts along Chicago River begin
entries.summary: <p>It's time for boaters to move their vessels to storage as fall bridge lifts along the Chicago River are beginning Wednesday the Chicago Department of Transportation announced. </p><p>Each spring and fall, CDOT raises the bridges along the Chicago River on a scheduled basis to accommodate recreational boats traveling between Lake Michigan and storage yards along the river.</p><p>During the boat runs, bridges will be lifted in succession from DuSable Lake Shore Drive to the 18th Street Bridge on the South Branch of the Chicago River. They are typically raised one at a time, with each bridge lift taking an average of 8 to 12 minutes.</p><p>The fall lifts begin Wednesday at 9:30 a.m. and typically take place on Wednesdays and Saturdays, with limited schedule changes this fall to accommodate ongoing work on the Lake Street Bridge, the department said in a press release.</p><p>Motorists beware, delays were expected at bridges from DuSable Lake Shore Drive to 18th Street for the lifts, the Office of Emergency Management and Communications said in an alert. </p><p>Here is the full lift schedule: <br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-af6b4772-bcd7-11f1-b303-e965590644dc"><li>Wednesday, September 30 at 9:30 a.m.</li><li>Saturday, October 3 at 9:00 a.m.</li><li>Wednesday, October 7 at 9:30 a.m.</li><li>Saturday, October 10 at 9:00 a.m.</li><li>Saturday, October 17 at 9:00 a.m.</li><li>Tuesday, October 27 at 9:30 a.m.</li><li>Thursday, October 29 at 9:30 a.m.</li><li>Saturday, October 31 at 9:00 a.m.</li><li>Wednesday, November 4 at 9:30 a.m.</li><li>Saturday, November 7 at 9:00 a.m.</li><li>Saturday, November 14 at 9:00 a.m.</li></ul>

The Council approved the deal by a 46-3 vote.</p><p><b>What Chicago gets</b>: The new deal calls for the city to receive a $75 million transfer fee at closing, 5% of net income going forward, and 2% of the sale price if the meters are sold again before the deal ends in 2084. Daley</a>.</p><p><b>In other news</b>: The Council also on Tuesday <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydjhhrlt-l-n/" target="_blank" >voted to require future borrowing to be approved by a three-fifths vote</a> — that's 30 votes instead of the current threshold of 26 votes. entries.title: Cops release video of fatal gas station ambush in Greater Grand Crossing
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police have released video of a fatal gas station ambush in Greater Grand Crossing last week. </p><p>The video shows a black car pulling into a gas station in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/26/man-fatally-shot-during-car-chase-in-grand-crossing" target="_blank" >7500 block of South Cottage Grove Avenue</a> around 7 p.m. Friday. Suddenly, two masked gunmen wearing dark clothing approached a parked black car with Naseem D. Stevens at the wheel and at least one of the gunmen fired through the driver's seat window, police said. </p><p>The other gunman was shooting what appeared to be a machine gun near a gas pump at the lot, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p8fEfH4FJbQ" target="_blank" >the video</a>. </p><p>The masked gunmen then got back in the sedan before fleeing, officials said. </p><p>Stevens, 26, drove away when the other vehicle followed and shot at him in traffic, police said. After being shot, Stevens crashed near 73rd Street and Cottage Grove Avenue, according to a police report obtained by the Sun-Times.</p><p>A female passenger who was inside Stevens' vehicle fled following the crash, but she was not shot, according to the report. </p><p>A funeral sticker was on Stevens' vehicle, according to the report, which said the funeral for Chicago Rapper <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/13/homicide-fuller-park" target="_blank" >Bloodhound Q50 </a>was earlier in the day in Merrillville, Ind. but it was "uncertain" if the attack that left Stevens dead was linked. </p><p>Anyone with information on the shooting is encouraged to reach out to 312-747-8271. </p>

entries.title: Matrícula de las Escuelas Públicas de Chicago vuelve a caer, la cifra más baja en dos décadas
entries.summary: <p>La matrícula de las Escuelas Públicas de Chicago (CPS) volvió a caer, esta vez por 11,500 estudiantes, hasta los 304,700, informaron funcionarios el jueves al divulgar datos preliminares, la cifra más baja en más de dos décadas.</p><p>La matrícula se había estabilizado durante dos años —incluso subió brevemente— con la llegada de miles de estudiantes inmigrantes en 2023 y 2024. Pero la tendencia duró poco, ya que el desplome de 20 años en la matrícula del distrito se reanudó el año pasado y volvió a repetirse este otoño, alejándose de su pico de casi 439,000 estudiantes en el ciclo escolar 2002-2003.</p><p>La disminución de la matrícula —y, en consecuencia, las escuelas con poca inscripción— se ha convertido en un tema clave en la primera contienda en la historia de la ciudad por la presidencia de la junta escolar, pues algunos candidatos sugieren revisar los cierres de escuelas. El distrito mantiene una moratoria sobre los cierres hasta después de este ciclo escolar. Grupos comunitarios se concentraron la mañana del jueves pasado para pedir que la prohibición se extienda.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a Donald Trump.</p><p>“Esta es la conclusión: lo que controlamos es la calidad de la educación y la experiencia que brindamos a nuestros estudiantes”, dijo Macquline King, superintendente/directora ejecutiva”.</p><p>King dijo que el lado positivo es que, pese a otra caída, CPS recuperó su posición como el tercer sistema escolar público más grande del país.</p><p>“Sé que suena como ganar porque en marzo.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Archivo Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Tendencias de larga data y de amplio alcance</h3><p>Los líderes intentaron contextualizar la caída mostrando que la matrícula de las escuelas públicas está bajando en todo el país, especialmente en grandes distritos urbanos. Del 2014 al 2024, las mayores pérdidas de matrícula se han registrado en Los Ángeles, Houston, Chicago, Dallas y Filadelfia, según datos presentados por funcionarios de CPS.</p><p>Illinois también ha perdido unos 200,000 estudiantes de escuelas públicas en todo el estado, o el 10%, desde 2017.</p><p>Anniese Lewis, subdirectora de educación de CPS, dijo que los distritos escolares todavía no se han recuperado de las fuertes caídas durante la pandemia de COVID-19.</p><p>Lewis citó la caída de la natalidad a nivel nacional, que es “aún más pronunciada aquí en Chicago”.</p><p>En 2005, hubo unos 45,000 nacimientos en Chicago. Esa cifra cayó más del 40% a alrededor de 27,000 en 2023. El grupo de kínder del distrito se ha reducido por miles.</p><p>“Más recientemente, hemos caído por debajo del promedio nacional”, dijo Lewis a la junta el jueves.</p><p>El distrito tiene 450,000 cupos disponibles en sus escuelas, comparado a 455,000 niños en edad escolar en Chicago en 2024, el año del conteo más reciente. Con una ligera alza en la proporción de estudiantes de Chicago inscritos en escuelas privadas o clasificados en los datos del censo como “no inscritos” —lo que incluye a niños educados en casa, que abandonaron la escuela o que están entre una escuela y otra—, CPS se ha quedado con más asientos vacíos.</p><p>Entre el 2008 y el 2018, CPS atendía aproximadamente al 75% de la población en edad escolar de la ciudad. Para 2023, esa cifra había bajado al 71%, según un informe del grupo de defensa Kids First Chicago.</p><p>Las mayores caídas de la última década se han dado en algunos de los centros de comunidades inmigrantes de Chicago, como Pilsen, La Villita, Avondale, Brighton Park, Gage Park y McKinley Park, donde en algunos casos se han registrado reducciones de hasta 53% en los últimos 10 años, según CPS.</p><p>“Ha habido una rápida gentrificación que ha provocado una fuerte caída de la población juvenil. Las viviendas familiares multigeneracionales se están convirtiendo en casas unifamiliares, lo que reduce la disponibilidad de vivienda para familias”, dijo Lewis. “[Y] ha habido un éxodo de familias de clase trabajadora que se mudan a los suburbios exteriores en busca de casas unifamiliares y de una percepción de mayor seguridad”.</p><p>Al parecer, esas tendencias se aceleraron con la campaña de deportaciones perjudicial de la administración de Trump el otoño pasado. Algunos estudiantes fueron detenidos, y la actividad federal alrededor de las escuelas sembró el miedo en comunidades inmigrantes. Se registraron aumentos en el ausentismo entre los estudiantes de inglés que decidieron quedarse en casa durante los operativos. Algunas familias consideraron irse de la ciudad para escapar de la amenaza.</p><p>“Aunque Estados Unidos recibió una avalancha de nuevos llegados en 2023 y 2024, esa tendencia ahora se ha revertido drásticamente”, dijo Lewis. “Todos conocemos los cambios en la política migratoria y en la aplicación de la ley migratoria a nivel federal. Están llegando menos personas a Estados Unidos y más se están yendo”.</p><p>En Kelly College Prep, en Brighton Park, la matrícula de este año cayó en 229 estudiantes, a 1,273, según datos preliminares.</p><p>Mientras tanto, en los últimos 10 años la matrícula de CPS ha aumentado, en algunos casos de manera significativa, en áreas más acomodadas como O’Hare, el Loop, Lincoln Park, North Center, Near South Side y Kenwood.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-266f03" negros, blancos y asiáticoestadounidenses se mantuvo más o menos igual entre los 304,687 estudiantes inscritos en CPS en el día 20 del ciclo escolar, cuando el distrito realiza su conteo anual.</p><p>La proporción de estudiantes en educación especial volvió a crecer, a 18.4%. Pero el distrito contó ligeramente menos estudiantes en situación de pobreza, sin hogar o aprendiendo inglés, aunque los funcionarios dijeron que esas cifras suelen subir después del inicio del ciclo escolar, cuando se identifican las necesidades de los estudiantes.</p><p>Las escuelas chárter y contractuales registraron caídas de matrícula ligeramente más pronunciadas que las escuelas administradas por el distrito, en parte porque cinco antiguas escuelas chárter de Acero y ChiArts pasaron a ser escuelas tradicionales de CPS.</p><h3>Cierres de escuelas y la contienda por la presidencia de la junta</h3><p>Desde el muy controversial e histórico cierre de 50 escuelas ordenado por el exalcalde Rahm Emanuel en 2013, los cierres han sido una política explosiva que la mayoría de los líderes ha evitado proponer.</p><p>Pero esas conversaciones se reavivaron en la contienda de este año por la presidencia de la junta escolar, y tres de los cuatro candidatos indicaron, o dijeron abiertamente, que considerarían cerrar escuelas.</p><p>Un candidato, Victor P. Henderson, respondió a un cuestionario de candidatos de WBEZ, Sun-Times y Chalkbeat diciendo que consideraría cerrar escuelas “como último recurso extraordinario”. Sendhil Revuluri dijo que también estaría dispuesto a cerrar escuelas para mejorar la experiencia de los estudiantes en planteles que se han vuelto demasiado pequeños para atender sus necesidades académicas y sociales.</p><p>La aspirante y actual integrante de la junta, Jessica Biggs, se negó a responder sí o no, y en su lugar dijo que los cierres deberían ser “lo último” que propongan los líderes, pero que “la presión presupuestaria es real”. Sólo Hilario Domínguez, respaldado por el Sindicato de Maestros de Chicago (CTU), dijo que se opondría al cierre de escuelas.</p><p>Las pruebas han demostrado que los cierres de 2013 no redujeron los costos, no mejoraron los resultados de los estudiantes ni las condiciones en las comunidades, encontró el Sun-Times y WBEZ <a class="Link" href="https://graphics.suntimes.com/education/2023/chicagos-50-closed-schools/" target="_blank" >en una investigación una década después.</a></p><p>“Tenemos 25 años de datos que demuestran el daño causado por cerrar escuelas y las personas a las que se apunta cuando cierran escuelas”, dijo el integrante de la junta Jitu Brown, quien participó en una huelga de hambre en 2015 para evitar el cierre de una escuela del lado sur. “Más del 80% de los cierres de escuelas en Estados Unidos han ocurrido en vecindarios negros. Eso significa que las comunidades negras han sido señaladas. Y por eso, humildemente, les pido que seamos diferentes, que veamos las escuelas consideradas menos utilizadas con una perspectiva distinta, como una oportunidad.</p><p>“Espero que [cerrar escuelas] no sea lo que está sobre la mesa”.</p><p><i>Contribuyó: Nicole Jeanine Johnson </i></p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Arts Alliance Illinois calls on Mayor Brandon Johnson to boost arts by $15 million in FY27
entries.summary: <p>The statewide arts advocacy group Arts Alliance Illinois is calling on Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson to boost cultural funding in the next budget.</p><p>In an <a class="Link" href="https://artsalliance.org/advocacy/fy27-chicago-budget/" target="_blank" ><u>open letter to the mayor</u></a>, the group says it wants the city to increase the grantmaking budget at the Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events, which gives funding directly to artists and arts organizations, by $15 million.</p><p>How much cities and states contribute to the arts has become a key question among cultural leaders as federal funding priorities <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts-culture/2025/05/06/nea-grants-trump-chicago-cultural-events" target="_blank" ><u>have shifted</u></a> under President Donald Trump. Last year, DCASE awarded a total of $10.8 million in grants to artists and arts organizations across a number of programs, according to public records. Recipients included everything from large companies like the Joffrey Ballet to the South Side storefront Perceptions Theatre.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div capita arts dollars, Chicago was the only among the country’s five largest cities (New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, Houston and Phoenix) to cut the funding for its local arts agency during its most recent budget cycle. DCASE <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/city-hall/2025/11/05/chicago-dcase-cultural-affairs-budget-clinee-hedspeth-kenya-merritt-grants-arts" target="_blank" ><u>took a 15% cut</u></a> in the 2026 budget.</p><p>Now, Arts Alliance is calling on Johnson to reverse the trend and is asking local cultural workers to sign on to its open letter, which they say they will share with the mayor as his administration develops next year’s budget proposal.</p><p>The group acknowledged the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/city-hall/2026/09/03/mayor-brandon-johnson-2027-budget-forecast-chicago-city-hall-deficit" target="_blank" ><u>budget hardships</u></a> the city faces, but argues that “investment in the arts should be a key part of Chicago’s FY2027 economic strategy.”</p><p>“As the City develops its FY27 budget, we ask you to demonstrate that commitment through restoring investment in the artists and cultural organizations that make Chicago great,” the letter reads. “DCASE’s direct grantmaking programs serve as a key source of support for our neighborhoods.”</p><p>The advocacy group said local investment is especially needed at a time when <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2025/05/03/nx-s1-5385888/sweeping-cuts-hit-nea-after-trump-administration-calls-to-eliminate-the-agency" target="_blank" ><u>federal arts support</u></a> has withered under the Trump administration. Private foundations have also shifted priorities elsewhere.</p><p>The group also pointed to the economic impact of the arts sector, including a study it released this summer that found Chicago’s creative economy is the city’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts-culture/2026/06/25/creative-economy-impact-study-arts-alliance-illinois-workers" target="_blank" ><u>third-largest industry</u></a>.</p><p>“Government support of arts and culture is felt not only in our theaters, our community art centers, and our studios,” the letter reads. “But across shared priorities including violence prevention, youth development, education, public health, and community building.”</p><p><i>Courtney Kueppers is an arts and culture reporter at WBEZ. </i></p>

entries.title: Police warn of attempted child luring near Parkway Gardens complex
entries.summary: <p>Police are looking for the person responsible for an attempted child luring of a girl walking to school Tuesday morning along the stretch of King Drive known as O Block, which has become synonymous with street violence in Chicago. </p><p>The incident happened sometime between 9:30 a.m. and 10 a.m. Tuesday in the 6300 to 6500 block of South Martin Luther King Jr. Drive, police said. </p><p>The 6400 block King Drive is known as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2025/08/29/chicago-crime-violence-o-block-oblock-parkway-gardens-donald-trump-national-guard" target="_blank" >O Block</a>, a name that has become synonymous with street violence in Chicago. The block is home to the Parkway Gardens low-income apartment complex.</p><p>A girl was walking when she was followed for "several" blocks by a man driving a black sedan offering her money to approach the car, officials said. </p><p>The girl was able to get help from security officers and the man drove north on King Drive, according to police. </p><p>The man is believed to be between 30 and 35 years old with dark complexion and dreads, police said. He is believed to be between 5-foot-9 and 5-foot-11 and was wearing a black sweatshirt and black pants.</p><p>Anyone with information is encouraged to contact Area1 detectives at 312-747-8380 or submit an anonymous tip at <a class="Link" href="http://CPDTIP.com" target="_blank" >CPDTIP.com</a> and use reference JK-431584.</p>

entries.title: CPS cancels multiple football games after referees strike over nonpayment
entries.summary: <p>Chicago Public Schools has canceled multiple freshman and junior varsity football games this week after football referees went on strike due to not being paid for several weeks.</p><p>“Varsity [football] games are in jeopardy,” official Breyion Hutchinson told the Sun-Times on Wednesday. “If the officials are not paid today they will not work tomorrow.”</p><p>All the officials that regularly work CPS football games are on strike. According to official Mike Outten there are a couple hundred football officials.</p><p>"CPS officials can work two football games on Thursday, two games on Friday and up to three games on Saturday," Hutchinson said. "Along with volleyball and flag football. We depend on this money for our livelihood."</p><p>Football officials were paid directly by the schools for Weeks 1 through 3. CPS was supposed to start paying them in Week 4 and that hasn't happened according to Hutchinson and Outten. Week 7 begins on Thursday.</p><p>“Two weeks ago when we met with the [CPS Sports Administration] they told us funds would be released Friday through Monday,” Hutchinson said. “Then we received an email from [CPS Sports Director] Devon Morales on Monday which said funds were being released that day. That wasn’t true."</p><p>Morgan Park football coach Chris James confirmed to the Sun-Times that Morgan Park's freshman game on Monday and junior varsity game on Wednesday were canceled by CPS.</p><p>“As a staff and school we just want it to get worked out, this hurts the development of the players and the experience they have playing football,” James said.</p><p>Young football coach Dan Finger told the Sun-Times that Young's junior varsity game was canceled on Monday. Finger is concerned about the status of his varsity game on Thursday against Bulls Prep.</p><p>“It is frustrating because with a little heads up we’d pay for the refs ourselves,” Finger said. “Junior varsity only gets five games or so to begin with and we didn’t find out [it was canceled] until 2 p.m. with kickoff at 4:30 p.m.”</p><p>Ten varsity Public League football games are scheduled for Thursday with a full slate of games scheduled on Friday and Saturday.</p><p>CPS has not released any statement on the issue.</p><p>"Our stance is until these guys are paid they are not going on the field," Outten said. "We had a meeting on Monday in which we asked the officials who has been paid. Everyone said they had not. We aren’t working until they pay us."</p><p>Illinois High School Association Executive Director Craig Anderson released the following statement on Wednesday.</p><p>“The IHSA is aware of the current situation between Chicago Public Schools (CPS) and IHSA football officials working games for CPS. Given that IHSA officials are hired as independent contractors, we have no direct involvement in this matter but are monitoring it closely. Officials have a difficult job, and at a time when it is becoming more difficult to recruit and retain officials, it is vital that they be provided the respect they deserve in every step of the process. We expect the situation will be remedied expeditiously so our officials are justly compensated for their work, and student-athletes do not have to miss out on any participation opportunities. We are ready and willing to be a resource in any way we can to help resolve this matter.”</p><p>State Rep. Kam Buckner also released a statement on Wednesday. </p><p>"Administrative problems happen," Buckner said in the statement. "Payment systems fail. Invoices get delayed.
